lessons.title: Tables, Rows, Columns, and Data Types
lessons.summary: A relational table represents a set of rows with named typed columns.
lessons.body:
Tables, Rows, Columns, and Data Types

Why this matters
A relational table represents a set of rows with named typed columns. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• A relational table represents a set of rows with named typed columns.
• Choose types that match domain meaning and constraints, not just whatever accepts the current example.
• NULL means missing/unknown, not empty string or zero.
• Schema design determines which invalid states the database can prevent.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, databases and sql primer stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter tables, rows, columns, and data types again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, and Relationships
lessons.summary: Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys state that a referenced parent must exist.
lessons.body:
Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, and Relationships

Why this matters
Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys state that a referenced parent must exist. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys state that a referenced parent must exist.
• One-to-many places the foreign key on the many side; many-to-many uses a relation/join table.
• Composite keys/unique constraints can encode business identity such as one membership per user/workspace.

lessons.title: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
lessons.summary: SELECT describes which rows/columns to read; WHERE filters; ORDER BY makes sequence explicit.
lessons.body:
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE

Why this matters
SELECT describes which rows/columns to read; WHERE filters; ORDER BY makes sequence explicit. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• SELECT describes which rows/columns to read; WHERE filters; ORDER BY makes sequence explicit.

lessons.title: Joins, Grouping, and Aggregation
lessons.summary: INNER JOIN keeps matching rows; LEFT JOIN preserves left rows even without a match.
lessons.body:
Joins, Grouping, and Aggregation

Why this matters
INNER JOIN keeps matching rows; LEFT JOIN preserves left rows even without a match. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• INNER JOIN keeps matching rows; LEFT JOIN preserves left rows even without a match.
• Predict cardinality before joining or aggregation results can surprise you.
• GROUP BY forms groups before aggregate functions such as count/sum/min/max.
• Application reports often combine joins and aggregation; correctness comes before ORM syntax.

Transactions and Indexes

Why this matters
A transaction groups operations so atomicity/consistency expectations can be preserved. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• A transaction groups operations so atomicity/consistency expectations can be preserved.
• Indexes add alternate lookup structures that can speed reads but cost storage and write work.
• Index columns/order should follow actual query predicates/sorts.
• EXPLAIN provides evidence about plan choices; do not guess performance only from schema.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, databases and sql primer stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter transactions and indexes again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.body:
Lab: Transactions and Indexes

Purpose
This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Wrap two dependent writes in a transaction, force the second to fail, verify rollback, then compare a query plan before and after a relevant index.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

Definition of done
You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.
